title: Ngân sách trường và hoàn cảnh học sinh · Discuss both views
prompt: Some people support giving disadvantaged schools more funding per pupil than affluent schools, while others oppose it because of the risks it could create. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Dạng discuss yêu cầu giải thích riêng vì sao mỗi phía tin lập trường của mình rồi đưa phán đoán của người viết. Trong bài này, cân nhắc trọng tâm là: Cùng tiền trên đầu học sinh không tạo cùng khả năng học nếu nhu cầu ban đầu khác nhau. Nhân sự ngôn ngữ giúp trường giải quyết rào cản học tập mà không cắt ngân sách môn khác. Tiền có thể dừng ở quản trị thay vì đến lớp. Gắn khoản chi với hỗ trợ được cung cấp và đo tiến bộ từ điểm xuất phát xử lý đúng vấn đề; xếp hạng điểm tuyệt đối có thể phạt trường nhận học sinh khó khăn.
outline.content: Supporters argue that weighted funding can compensate for unequal educational starting points. Opponents respond that additional money can be absorbed by administration without changing classroom practice. I favour unequal allocations that reflect unequal needs, while accepting that opponents' concerns about waste require evidence of additional classroom support and progress rather than simply larger budgets.

paragraphs: Supporters argue that weighted funding can compensate for unequal educational starting points. Opponents respond that additional money can be absorbed by administration without changing classroom practice. I favour unequal allocations that reflect unequal needs, while accepting that opponents' concerns about waste require evidence of additional classroom support and progress rather than simply larger budgets.

Weighted funding can compensate for unequal educational starting points. Smaller support groups and specialist staff help schools address barriers that ordinary classroom teaching cannot resolve. A school serving newly arrived families might employ language specialists rather than reduce its science budget. Otherwise, meeting a language need may require diverting money from subjects that every pupil still needs, reproducing disadvantage inside the school's ordinary budget. Additional funding is useful only when schools can turn it into relevant support, such as language teaching, rather than merely expanding administrative expenditure.

Additional money can be absorbed by administration without changing classroom practice. Allocating money does not determine what happens inside a classroom. Weak needs assessment or poor purchasing decisions can absorb a larger budget, so expenditure rises while the barriers preventing pupils from learning remain essentially unchanged. Funding should be linked to identified needs and evaluated through progress rather than raw examination rankings. The relevant audit asks what support reached classrooms and whether comparable pupils improved, not merely whether the school spent its additional allocation. Evaluation should examine pupils' progress from their starting points and the support actually delivered, not compare raw examination scores alone.

Equal allocations overlook the unequal cost of participation, but larger allocations do not prove better teaching; weighted funding combined with evidence of pupil progress best reconciles fairness with financial accountability.
